## Publications

**Myers, C. D.** (2025). *Politicizing the Pandemic? Partisan Framing of the Early COVID-19 Pandemic Was Infrequent, Particularly in Local Newspapers*. *Political Communication*. [https://doi.org/10.1080/10584609.2024.2372593](https://doi.org/10.1080/10584609.2024.2372593)  
**Abstract:** Media scholars have long expressed concern that news outlets’ tendency to frame policy debates in terms of partisan conflict or political gamesmanship politicizes and polarizes public opinion. This tendency may be particularly problematic with new, highly salient issues like the COVID-19 pandemic during its earliest stages. To evaluate the degree to which coverage of the pandemic in its first months was framed in partisan terms, the study analyzes the content of COVID-19 related articles published on the front pages of the *New York Times*, *Washington Post*, and a random sample of local newspapers between February 21 and May 15, 2020. Contrary to expectations, these newspapers employed partisan framings in only about one out of ten articles. However, frequencies vary dramatically by type of newspaper: national papers were much more likely than local ones to use partisan framing, and among local papers, higher-circulation outlets were more likely than lower-circulation ones. These findings suggest that the degree to which news consumers perceive partisan framing depends on whether they consume local or national media, and that the decline of local news outlets may have contributed to increased exposure to partisan portrayals early in the pandemic.

**Busby, E., Howat, A., & Myers, C. D.** (2024). *Changing Partisan Stereotypes in the Trump Era*. *Political Science Research and Methods*. [https://doi.org/10.1017/psrm.2023.30](https://doi.org/10.1017/psrm.2023.30)  
**Abstract:** Stereotypes of the two major political parties play a significant role in political cognition, yet little research has examined how these stereotypes evolve over time. This study compares open-ended responses (from 2016 and 2021) in which individuals list descriptive words about party members. Using a structural topic model, the analysis reveals that by 2021, partisan stereotypes had shifted away from group- or issue-based descriptions, and became more focused on personal traits. These evolving perceptions suggest that during the Trump era, the public increasingly viewed political parties in personalized, character-focused terms—potentially contributing to affective polarization.
